changes.before: Embed the harmless note using srcdoc, give the frame a title, and keep an empty sandbox attribute with no permission tokens.
changes.after: Show a small embedded page with its permissions kept restricted.

before: iframe embeds a separate document. Its title helps identify the frame to assistive technology.

srcdoc supplies inline HTML instead of fetching an external page.
```html
<iframe title="Example note" sandbox srcdoc="<p>A quiet note.</p>"></iframe>
```
An empty sandbox attribute enables restrictions without granting optional permissions. Omitting sandbox is not the same as writing it empty.
Permission tokens can relax specific restrictions. This exercise needs no scripts, forms, popups or same-origin access, so it grants none.
Do not combine allow-scripts and allow-same-origin casually for same-origin untrusted content; that can undermine the intended restriction.
Sandboxing is not sanitization or a blanket network firewall. Treat HTML input deliberately, use a suitable content policy, and grant only the abilities actually needed.
The practice uses only fixed, harmless text. Its checks inspect the embedding contract, not every browser security boundary or arbitrary hostile document.
after: `<iframe>` shows a separate page inside your page. Give it a clear `title` so someone using a screen reader can tell what the frame contains.

`srcdoc` holds the small page’s HTML directly.

```html
<iframe title="Example note" sandbox srcdoc="<p>A quiet note.</p>"></iframe>
```

The title names the frame. Inside srcdoc, `<` and `>` represent the tag brackets. The embedded page displays one paragraph. The empty sandbox attribute adds restrictions.
`sandbox` limits what the embedded page can do. Keeping the attribute empty turns those restrictions on without granting extra permissions. Leaving the attribute out does not do the same thing.
Words inside sandbox can grant specific permissions. This note needs no scripts, forms or popup windows, so it does not need any permission words.

Be careful with `allow-scripts` and `allow-same-origin` together. For untrusted content from your own site, that combination can let the embedded page escape the intended restrictions. This exercise uses neither.

Sandbox restrictions do not remove unwanted HTML or block every network request. For this exercise, use only the supplied fixed note. Do not treat the example as a complete way to protect against any possible embedded page.
Keep the starter title and srcdoc unchanged. Add `sandbox` with no value or permission words. Run the checks. They verify this small frame’s settings and text.

before.question: An iframe has sandbox="". You remove the entire attribute. Is the result still equally restricted?
choices: Yes, both contain no permission words
No, removing sandbox removes those sandbox restrictions

before.explanation: The presence of sandbox enables its restrictions. An empty value grants no optional permissions; absence does not enable sandboxing.

after.question: You remove sandbox="" from an iframe. Does it keep the same restrictions?
choices: Yes. Both versions have no permission words.
No. Removing the attribute removes its sandbox restrictions.
Yes. Srcdoc always turns sandbox on.
after.explanation: The presence of sandbox turns the restrictions on. An empty value adds no extra permissions.
